common_name: Guernsey Cream Clematis (Pale Cream-Yellow Large-Flowered Clematis)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Guernsey Cream blooms on old wood in late spring, so prune only lightly to remove dead or weak stems.

directions: Plant with roots shaded and cool while the vine climbs into full sun to light shade on a trellis or fence. Guernsey Cream bears large, pale cream-yellow flowers with a soft, gentle tone unusual among large-flowered clematis hybrids, which lean heavily toward blues, purples, and pinks, making it a distinctive choice for a pastel or all-white garden scheme. Because it flowers mainly on old wood from the previous season, limit pruning to removing dead or damaged stems in late winter rather than cutting the whole plant back hard. It has been a garden favorite for its unusual color and dependable, large-scale bloom.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; H.F. Young blooms on old wood in late spring, so prune only lightly to remove dead or weak stems.

directions: Plant with roots shaded and cool while the vine climbs into full sun to light shade on a trellis or fence. H.F. Young bears large, clear mid-blue flowers with cream-colored stamens, a clean, true blue considered one of the finest of its color class among large-flowered clematis hybrids. Because it flowers mainly on old wood from the previous season, limit pruning to removing dead or damaged stems in late winter rather than cutting the whole plant back hard. Its reliable, large blooms and award-winning garden performance have kept it a long-standing favorite.

common_name: Vyvyan Pennell Clematis (Double Violet-Blue Early-Season Clematis)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Vyvyan Pennell produces double flowers on old wood in late spring and single flowers on new growth later in the season.

directions: Plant with roots shaded and cool while the vine climbs into full sun to light shade on a trellis or fence. Vyvyan Pennell is unusual for producing two distinct flower forms in a single season: fully double, violet-blue rosette-like blooms from old wood in late spring, followed by simpler single flowers in a similar color on new growth later in summer. This dual bloom pattern means pruning strategy matters more than with most clematis, so limit spring pruning to dead or weak stems in order to preserve the spectacular early double display. Its extended, two-phase bloom season has made it a favorite among clematis collectors.

common_name: Madame Julia Correvon Clematis (Wine-Red Nodding Viticella Clematis)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Madame Julia Correvon is a viticella-type clematis that blooms on new growth and can be cut back hard each late winter.

directions: Plant with roots shaded and cool while the vine climbs into full sun on a trellis or through a shrub. Madame Julia Correvon bears an abundance of nodding, wine-red flowers with slightly twisted petals over a long summer season, on a vigorous vine well suited to scrambling through a large shrub or covering a fence quickly. As a viticella-group clematis it flowers on the current season's growth, so it can be cut back hard to about a foot from the ground each late winter, a far simpler pruning routine than the large-flowered old-wood types. Its rich color and easy care have made it one of the most popular viticella cultivars.

common_name: Alba Luxurians Clematis (White with Green-Tipped Petals Viticella Clematis)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Alba Luxurians is a viticella-type clematis that blooms on new growth and can be cut back hard each late winter.

directions: Plant with roots shaded and cool while the vine climbs into full sun on a trellis or through a shrub. Alba Luxurians bears nodding white flowers, each petal tip touched with soft green and often twisted into an irregular, informal shape, a subtle novelty coloring distinct from the solid white typical of most white clematis. As a viticella-group clematis it flowers on the current season's growth, so the entire vine can be cut back hard to about a foot from the ground in late winter, avoiding the guesswork of pruning old-wood types. Its abundant, quirky flowers bloom over a long midsummer season.

common_name: Elizabeth Clematis Montana (Vigorous Fragrant Pale Pink Spring Clematis)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Elizabeth is an extremely vigorous spring-blooming Clematis montana selection needing a very sturdy, large support.

directions: Plant with roots shaded and cool while the vine climbs into full sun to light shade on a large, sturdy support such as a pergola, fence, or mature tree. Elizabeth produces an overwhelming single spring flush of small, soft pink, vanilla-scented flowers covering the entire vine, one of the most vigorous Clematis montana selections available and capable of climbing 20 feet or more in ideal conditions. It flowers on the previous year's growth, so prune only right after bloom to control size, never in winter or spring, which would remove the coming display. Its enormous mature size makes it best suited to a large property where it can cover a substantial structure rather than a small garden bed.

common_name: Frances Rivis Clematis (Nodding Blue Bell-Flowered Alpine Clematis)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Frances Rivis is a compact, early-spring-blooming alpine clematis suited to smaller supports.

directions: Plant with roots shaded and cool while the vine climbs into full sun to light shade on a modest trellis or through a small shrub. Frances Rivis bears nodding, bell-shaped, blue flowers with twisted petals very early in spring, ahead of most other clematis, followed by decorative fluffy seedheads that extend interest into summer. Its more compact, restrained growth compared to large-flowered hybrids and montana types makes it a good choice for smaller gardens or containers. Prune only lightly right after flowering to shape, since it blooms on the previous year's growth.

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in late winter or early spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Bailey Compact is a smaller-growing selection of American cranberrybush viburnum.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. Bailey Compact is a smaller-growing selection of the native American cranberrybush, bearing flat clusters of white spring flowers followed by bright red, tart, cranberry-like fruit that persists into winter and draws birds, all on a shrub considerably more compact than the straight species. Its manageable size fits foundation plantings and smaller landscapes better than full-size cranberrybush viburnum, while still producing a good crop of ornamental and wildlife-friendly fruit. Prune lightly right after flowering if shaping is needed, since it blooms on the previous year's wood.

common_name: Mohican Viburnum (Compact Wayfaring Tree with Orange-Red Fruit)

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in late winter or early spring in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Mohican is a compact selection of wayfaring tree valued for heavy fruit set and disease resistance.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; wayfaring tree tolerates a wide range of soils including dry, alkaline sites better than many viburnum species. Mohican forms a dense, compact, rounded shrub bearing flat clusters of white spring flowers followed by a heavy crop of berries that shift dramatically from green to orange-red to black as they ripen, often showing all three colors in the same cluster for a striking display. It is notably tough and disease-resistant, tolerating urban conditions and drought well once established. Prune lightly right after flowering if shaping is needed, since it blooms on the previous year's wood.

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in late winter or early spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Onondaga is a Sargent viburnum selection with maroon-tinted new foliage and pink-tinted lacecap flowers.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. Onondaga emerges with striking maroon-purple new growth that matures to green with a maroon overlay, and bears flat lacecap flower clusters of white fertile florets rimmed by showy pink-tinted sterile florets, followed by red fruit that ripens to black. Its dramatic, multi-season foliage color sets it apart from most green-leaved viburnum species, making it a strong focal shrub in a mixed border. Prune lightly right after flowering if shaping is needed, since it blooms on the previous year's wood.

common_name: Pink Beauty Doublefile Viburnum (Lacecap White Aging to Pink)

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in late winter or early spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Pink Beauty is a doublefile viburnum selection whose white lacecap flowers age to pink.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. Pink Beauty bears flat, lacecap flower clusters held in two rows along horizontally tiered branches, the classic doublefile viburnum form, opening white and gradually aging to soft pink as the blooms mature, so a single plant can show both colors at once during peak bloom. Its strong horizontal branching habit gives it striking architectural structure even out of bloom, and red fruit follows in summer. Prune lightly right after flowering to maintain the tiered branch structure, since it blooms on the previous year's wood.
